claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is a homogenized, single-phase solid solution in the tested initial state.
The strength–ductility behavior of Co-free FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain rate is governed primarily by solid-solution strengthening together with effects associated with Co absence.
The absence of Co suppresses stacking-fault formation.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Co content modulates stacking-fault energy and dislocation mobility in the FCC lattice.
Lower stacking-fault energy restricts dislocation cross-slip.
Lower stacking-fault energy increases planar slip.
Restricted cross-slip and increased planar slip stabilize ductility, particularly at elevated temperatures.
Restricted cross-slip and increased planar slip reduce strain-rate sensitivity, particularly at elevated temperatures.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have similar or slightly lower yield strength.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will retain comparable or greater ductility at elevated temperatures.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit lower strain-rate sensitivity of strength and ductility.
Relative to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit less pronounced dynamic strain aging.
The proposed mechanism applies only to a single-phase FCC solid-solution state and may not apply after secondary-phase formation or ordering.
The proposed applicable regime extends from room temperature to approximately 600°C and from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Equal or greater strain-rate sensitivity in Co-free FeNiCrMn than in CoCrFeMnNi would falsify the hypothesis.
A significant elevated-temperature ductility loss in Co-free FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says that Co absence suppresses stacking-fault formation while also saying that Co removal lowers stacking-fault energy. Lower stacking-fault energy ordinarily makes stacking-fault formation more favorable, so the stated suppression conflicts with the proposed mediator and planar-slip mechanism.
